titulo: Square desktop robot: rotating and tilting screen head, to print on the A1 — robos-impressos
meta: 20 cm square desktop robot with a screen on its face and a head that rotates and tilts. STL and 3MF files are already positioned for printing, with a shopping list that includes estimated prices and links, step-by-step assembly instructions, and a wire-by-wire wiring diagram.
hero_h1: Square desktop robot: rotating and tilting screen head, for you to print on the A1
hero_lead: You want a robot on your desk and don't want to get stuck halfway through: a screw is missing, a part doesn't fit in the printer, and nobody tells you what to buy or where each wire goes. Here, the files are already in print position, the list tells you what the robot uses and how much to buy, and the assembly takes you from the first threaded insert to the last wire.

resumo: The square robot is a [[N_ALTURA]] cm desktop robot that you can print at home and assemble. Its head is a cube with a 3.5-inch screen on its face; it rotates almost all the way around and tilts up and down. Inside are a Raspberry Pi, an Arduino, two servos, and a battery that charges via USB-C. You need a 3D printer with a 256 mm build plate, the parts on the shopping list, and a soldering iron. This page covers phase 1: the body assembled, the wires connected, and both servos centered. Programming (screen face, voice, camera, AI) is phase 2 and has not been done yet.

imp_sub: Bambu Lab A1, 0.4 mm nozzle, 0.2 mm layer. PETG for load-bearing parts, PLA for parts that only cover something.
imp_perfil: Suggestion for the A1, not yet tested with these parts: use the textured PEI plate for both materials. In Bambu Studio, choose the Generic PLA profile for PLA and Generic PETG for PETG, and keep the temperatures set by the profile. Typical values to check: PLA with the nozzle at 220 °C and the build plate at 55–65 °C; PETG with the nozzle at 250–255 °C and the build plate at 70–80 °C. Bambu’s filament guide lists 240 to 270 °C for the PETG nozzle (source).
imp1_p: It is on build plate 06, together with the 4 Raspberry Pi spacers. Test one threaded insert in each of the 3 holes (3.9, 4.0, and 4.1 mm), one M3 screw in the through-hole, and another in the hole for threading directly into the plastic. The dimple marks the size used by the project. The servo window and the coupon sockets are for the other robots in the project: check the MG996R servo fit in the head frame (build plate 01) and the M5 screw thread in the fork (build plate 03). The coupon is printed in PLA, and most inserts go into PETG parts: print a second coupon in PETG. It is not on any build plate or included in the totals: load the file comum-teste-encaixe.stl separately, using PETG, and allow about 15 g and 38 extra minutes. If another hole works better than the one marked by the dimple, you do not need to remake the parts: in Bambu Studio, the X-Y hole compensation option (X-Y hole compensation; Quality tab, Precision group, with advanced mode enabled) opens or closes all the holes in the part: a positive value opens them, a negative value closes them (source: Bambu Studio code). The source does not say whether the value applies per side or to the diameter: start with 0.05 mm and print the coupon again. Let the coupon decide. If you work with the code, you can change the value in comum/cad/parametros.py (the FOLGA block) and generate the parts again.

imp_nota_md: The same print guide, in text:
mon_sub: First, four workbench prep steps with the parts still loose: all the soldering happens here. Then assembly, in the same order the checker tested: each part goes in from the indicated side without hitting anything already assembled.
prep_p: These come first because, once the robot is closed, you can no longer reach the converter adjustment, the Arduino USB port, or the Raspberry Pi pins and card. All soldering on the robot is done here; assembly only uses screw terminals and fittings. Prep steps 1, 2, and 3 are electrical and have not been bench-tested: measure each connection with the multimeter before turning on the switch. The sequence is the same as in the wiring file, step by step.
prep1_p: Assemble the wiring harness following the wiring diagram, with the printed base beside you. Do not connect the Raspberry Pi, Arduino, or servos yet.
prep2_p: The program is the sketch centrar_servos.ino. It moves both servos to the middle point and keeps them there.
prep2_b: Do not power the MG996R servo through USB: it supplies 0,5 A, and the servo draws more when starting. Never connect the computer's USB cable while the battery is connected. Upload the sketch before screwing the Uno onto the base: once it is in place, the USB cable will not fit.
prep3_p: The Raspberry Pi goes in the head and the Arduino in the base. They communicate through 3 wires that run down the neck. Here you prepare these wires, with a low-profile connector at the Pi end, and assemble the 3-resistor divider that protects the Pi from the Arduino's 5 V. No more soldering is needed after this prep step.
prep3_b: Where pin 1 is and why the pin number is not the GPIO number: Raspberry Pi documentation. On a powered-on Pi, the pinout command draws a map of the pins. Pins 31 to 34 are beneath the display board, where about 17.5 mm remains (unconfirmed measurement): that is why the connector is low-profile and the wires come out flat.
prep4_p: The card is flashed on your computer with a microSD card reader. Then you connect to the Raspberry Pi over the network using SSH: you type commands on your computer, and they run on the Pi.
prep4_b: The display is the MPI3501 (ILI9486 controller, connected over SPI). Sources: MPI3501 page on lcdwiki (driver) and Raspberry Pi documentation on GitHub (SSH and how to find the Pi's address). Not bench-tested: the manufacturer lists tests up to the Raspberry Pi 3B+. Plan B, also not tested: instead of the script, add the line dtoverlay=piscreen,drm to the end of the /boot/firmware/config.txt file and restart (this is the official overlay for a 3.5-inch display with the same controller; the source does not guarantee that it works with the MPI3501). If none of this turns on the display, flash the card again with Raspberry Pi OS (Legacy) and repeat the manufacturer's script. The serial line comes from the Raspberry Pi firmware overlay list; after restarting, the port name appears with ls /dev/ttyAMA*.
prep_nota: Threaded inserts: set the iron between 220 and 250 °C, a little above the printing temperature for the part's plastic (typical value, NC). Place the tip inside the insert, let the heat soften the plastic, and slowly push without forcing it until the insert is flush with the surface. If your iron has no temperature control, apply heat for less time.
mon_paraf_t: Screws and inserts, one by one
mon_paraf_p: There are [[N_INSERTOS]] M3 heat-set inserts. Seat them all before you start assembling.
mon_passos_p: Steps marked (workbench) are done outside the robot, with the part in your hand.
mon_abrir_p: Replacing the battery or working on the boards does not require disassembling the head.
en_sub: Two 18650 batteries in series provide 6 to 8,4 V. From there, two separate lines supply 5,1 V to the Raspberry Pi and Arduino, and 6 V to the servos.
seg_li:
• None of this has been bench-tested. The wiring diagram is based on the component datasheets. Check each connection with a multimeter before turning on the switch.
  • Polarity: red to positive, black to negative. Measure before each new connection. Reversed wires burn out the board immediately.
  • Adjust before connecting the load: set the LM2596 to 5.1 V and the UBEC to 6 V, measured with a multimeter, with the Raspberry Pi, Arduino, and servos disconnected.
  • A short circuit can start a fire: solder with the cells OUT of the holder and insulate each splice with heat-shrink tubing. The 3 A fuse goes right after the holder.
  • Matching cells: use two new 18650 cells from the same brand and model. Take dented, swollen, or hot cells to a battery collection point, not the robot.
  • First charge: stay nearby, with the robot on a surface that won’t burn.
en_f3: LM2596: 5,1 V for the Raspberry Pi and Arduino · UBEC: 6 V for the 2 servos
en1_t: 5,1 V for the Raspberry Pi and Arduino
en1_p: The LM2596 converter keeps the 5 V output steady until the battery drops to about 6.5 V. Its output goes to a terminal block in the base. From there, one pair of 20 AWG wires runs up the neck to the Pi's USB-C adapter, and another pair goes to the + and − pins of the Sensor Shield's COM connector. The board can handle about 2 A continuously without a heatsink (typical value, NC): use the Pi 4, or the Pi 5 without USB accessories. If the Pi reports undervoltage (the vcgencmd get_throttled command returns anything other than throttled=0x0), shorten this pair of wires and check the 5.1 V.
en2_p: The UBEC supplies 3 A continuously to both MG996R servos through the Sensor Shield's blue screw terminal, with the SEL jumper removed. If the jumper were in place, the 6 V would flow into the Arduino's 5 V line. A 1000 µF capacitor at the terminal helps handle the startup surge.
en3_p: The balance charger sits with its port at a window behind the base and accepts a USB-C power supply up to 15 W. It needs a third wire, soldered to the point joining the two cells. It connects before the switch, so the robot charges while switched off.
en4_t: The Raspberry Pi and Arduino communicate over serial
en4_p: The Pi sits in the head and the Arduino in the base, and a USB plug won’t fit through the 9 mm neck hole. That’s why the connection uses a 3-wire serial link (UART): the Pi sends through pin 32 and listens on pin 33. These numbers are the pin positions in the 40-pin row, counted from the microSD card corner; they are not GPIO numbers. The Arduino runs at 5 V and the Pi at 3.3 V: 3 1 kΩ resistors, secured to the terminal block, lower the voltage on the wire from the Arduino to the Pi. On the Pi system, serial is enabled with a line in the configuration file: dtoverlay=uart5 on the Pi 4 or dtoverlay=uart4-pi5 on the Pi 5, always after the display script (prep step 4).
esq_p: Each box is a component, and each line is a wire in the indicated color. Click to open it at full size.
esq_img_alt: Wiring diagram: battery, fuse, protection board, charger, switch, converters, Arduino with Sensor Shield, servos, Raspberry Pi, and screen, with colored wires connecting them
lig_p: The same information as the diagram, with one line per wire. Names in parentheses are the ones usually printed on the boards; if your board uses a different name, follow the name on the board.
en_nota: Currents calculated from the datasheets, not measured. Normal use: about 2 A from the pack. Peak: about 5 A, with the LM2596 at 2 A, the UBEC at its 3 A limit, and the pack at 6,5 V. The KCD11-101 switch is rated for 3 A at 250 V~ and 6 A at 125 V~ (store listing), with no rating for direct current. That is why the fuse is 3 A, the switch's lowest rating, and slow-blow (marked T3A): servo startup and capacitor charging cause peaks lasting a fraction of a second that would blow a fast fuse without a fault. This keeps normal use below the rating, lets a seconds-long peak pass without blowing the fuse, and makes a sustained overload blow the fuse before the switch heats up (typical behavior for a glass fuse, NC). The phase 2 program must not let both servos push against their limits at the same time.

a_c1e2c34bc9: Reconnect the USB cable just to take a measurement with the multimeter. The shield's COM connector has 4 upright pins labeled TX, RX, −, and +. You should get about 5 V between + and −. On the D9 connector, you should get 0 V between the V pin and the G pin.
a_5d87ec2c20: If the D9 V pin reads 5 V, the SEL jumper is still in place. If the COM + pin does not read 5 V, your shield differs from the store photo: look for another pin labeled + or 5V that reads 5 V with SEL removed. A wrong pin here sends the servos' 6 V to the Raspberry Pi.
a_7a090fffa7: The UBEC output has a 3-pin servo plug: cut it off and strip the wires. Red is positive and black (or brown) is negative. If there’s a third wire, white or orange, insulate its end with heat-shrink tubing. Clamp the red wire into VCC and the black wire into GND on the blue screw terminal. The 1000 µF capacitor goes into the same terminal, with its longer lead in VCC.
a_8c6873572e: Take 2 40 cm jumper wires, cut the connector off one end of each, and strip the wires. Clamp one in terminal 1 of the terminal block, opposite the converter, and plug its connector into the + pin on the COM connector. Connect the other from terminal 2 to the − pin on the same connector. Leave the TX and RX pins beside it empty: 5 V on one of them reaches the Raspberry Pi through the serial wire.
a_29229d8384: Connect the pan servo to D9 and the tilt servo to D10: brown or black wire to G, red to V, orange or yellow to S.
a_68c1ef2667: Turn on the switch: both servos move to the center (90°) and the Uno LED blinks once per second.
a_09aa336173: Turn off the switch. From now on, do not turn the servo shafts by hand.
a_eb46901f51: Undo the test connections for assembly: remove the 2 servos from D9 and D10, disconnect the UBEC wires and capacitor from the blue screw terminal, and remove the 2 jumpers from the COM connector. If the shield covers the Uno mounting holes, remove it too. Take the 2 cells out of the holder: they go back in during assembly, at the battery step.
a_97daee9ad1: Make the serial cable and resistor divider
a_f9891efa36: With the wire cutters, cut a 2 × 2 piece from the female pin header: 2 rows with 2 holes each. This is the low-profile connector that goes on Raspberry Pi pins 31 to 34.
a_5c739999ad: Set aside 3 40 cm jumpers: one green, one blue, and one black (or mark 3 jumpers of another color with tape). Cut the connector off ONE end of each and strip 3 mm.
a_b0ca052182: Find the pins on the Raspberry Pi: pin 1 is at the corner next to the microSD card, on the inner row; pin 40 is at the opposite corner, on the outer row. Odd-numbered pins are on the inner row and even-numbered pins are on the outer row. Pins 31 and 32 are the 16th pair; pins 33 and 34 are the 17th.
a_8e50e3801a: Solder the 3 wire ends to the terminals of the 2 × 2 connector, with the wires lying flat and pointing to the side: green to the hole that will go on pin 32, blue to pin 33, black to pin 34. Leave the pin 31 terminal empty. Slide a piece of thin heat-shrink tubing over each solder joint.
a_8ca3d76349: Mark with a pen the corner of the connector where the empty terminal is, the one for pin 31. When you plug it in, the mark goes on the inner row, facing the microSD card. To check: there are 2 pairs of empty pins (27 to 30) between the connector and the display, and 3 pairs (35 to 40) on the other side. If the connector is reversed, it swaps the wires around.
a_08be24dae2: On the blue wire, also cut off the connector at the other end and strip 6 mm: this end goes into a screw terminal. Leave the green and black wires with their female connectors, which fit onto the shield.
a_d4dcf5609b: Now make the divider. Solder 2 1 kΩ resistors together, leg to leg, and cover the joint with heat-shrink tubing. This pair adds up to 2 kΩ.
a_25674cdbc6: Cut a jumper in half. Solder the cut end of one half to a leg of the 3rd resistor and cover it with heat-shrink tubing. The female connector on this half goes to D1.
a_20573e61bd: On the terminal block, on the converter side, tighten the free leg of the 3rd resistor together with one end of the 2 kΩ pair in terminal 3. Tighten the other end of the pair in terminal 2, together with the black wire already there. Bend the end of each leg before tightening, so the screw grips it.
a_6e60c32687: Check with the multimeter in ohms: between the D1 jumper’s female connector and terminal 3, about 1 kΩ; between terminal 3 and terminal 2, about 2 kΩ.
a_3dd5344a5c: Set the cable aside: the 2 × 2 connector plugs into the Raspberry Pi during assembly, before the display. At the base, the blue wire goes to terminal 3 on the terminal block, the green wire to the S pin of D0, and the black wire to the G pin of D0; use screw terminals or plug-in connections, no soldering. Attention: on the 3-pin connectors for D0 and D1, always leave the middle point (V) empty. With the SEL jumper removed, it carries the servos' 6 V, and 6 V on a serial wire will burn out the Raspberry Pi.
a_41ca9660b1: Flash the microSD card, install the screen driver, and connect the serial cable
a_2a0ce841a0: Install Raspberry Pi Imager, the free Raspberry Pi program, on your computer, and put the card in the reader.
a_8a000c1dec: In Imager, choose your Pi model, the Raspberry Pi OS (64-bit) operating system, and the card.
a_b92129aad4: Before flashing, open Imager’s settings: give the Pi a name (for example, `robo`), create a username and password, enter your Wi-Fi name and password, and enable SSH. Flash the card.
a_506c0f50f8: Put the card in the Pi, fit the screen onto pins 1 to 26 just for this test, and power on the Pi with a 5 V, 3 A USB-C power supply. Wait about 2 minutes.
a_dcfacd5ff1: On your computer, open the terminal: on Windows, use the PowerShell program; on Mac and Linux, use Terminal.
a_a1c155e74a: Type `ssh usuario@robo.local`, replacing `usuario` and `robo` with the names you created. Answer `yes` the first time and enter the password.
a_ffb9d37578: If `robo.local` doesn’t respond, open your router’s page, find the Pi in the list of connected devices, and use its number (the IP address), for example `ssh usuario@192.168.0.50`.
a_309915a0ad: When the terminal shows the Pi’s name, you’re inside it. Type the three driver commands, one per line, pressing Enter after each: `git clone https://github.com/goodtft/LCD-show.git`, then `cd LCD-show`, then `sudo ./LCD35-show`. The Pi needs internet access. It restarts on its own and the screen turns on.
a_e0b4846440: Connect again over SSH and enable the serial port AFTER the screen script, because it rewrites the configuration file. Type `sudo nano /boot/firmware/config.txt`, go to the end of the file, and add a line: `dtoverlay=uart5` on Raspberry Pi 4, or `dtoverlay=uart4-pi5` on Raspberry Pi 5. Save with Ctrl+O and Enter, then exit with Ctrl+X.
a_8e69e25605: Type `sudo poweroff`, wait for the Pi’s green LED to stop blinking, unplug the power supply, and detach the screen: you’ll put it back during assembly.
